key_terms.meaning: Deliberate pre-compression of concrete by a stretched tendon so the member carries tensile bending without cracking
The high-tensile steel wire, strand or bar that carries the prestressing force
The force applied by the jack at the anchorage at the moment of tensioning, in kN
Distance from the concrete centroidal axis to the tendon centroid, in mm
The load stage at which the pre-compression at the extreme tensile fibre is just used up and stress there becomes zero
The moment the prestressing force is passed from the jack or bed into the hardened concrete
Cold-drawn wire or 7-wire strand with tensile strength around 1500-1900 N/mm², used so large force fits in a small tendon
Tendons are stressed in a long bed against abutments before the concrete is cast and bonded
Concrete is cast first with a duct inside; the tendon is stressed afterwards and anchored against the concrete ends
The sheath that leaves a hole for the post-tensioned tendon; grout fills it later for bond and corrosion protection
Choosing a tendon profile whose upward equivalent load cancels part of the external load, so the beam bends little
Upward load from a parabolic tendon, w = 8 P e / L², in kN/m, where P is prestress, e sag at midspan and L span
The locus of the resultant compression at each section; its shift from the tendon line equals M/P
Loss because the concrete shortens when prestress is applied, taking the tendon along with it
Loss along a post-tensioned duct, P_x = P₀ e^(−μ(α + kx)), with μ friction coefficient, α angle change, k wobble, x length
Loss when the wedge or anchorage settles a few millimetres at transfer, shortening the tendon
Loss of tendon stress with time under constant strain, at constant length
The end block region, roughly one beam depth long, where the concentrated jacking force spreads into the full section
A tendon profile whose line coincides with the pressure line, giving no support reactions from prestress
Shifting a tendon profile by a straight line without changing the equivalent loads or the pressure line
Design that combines tendons with ordinary rebar so steel and prestress share strength and crack control

takeaways: Prestressing turns concrete's weakness in tension into an advantage by keeping the section in compression under service load.
Large forces are needed, so prestressed work demands high-strength concrete and high-tensile steel together.
Pre-tensioning relies on bond; post-tensioning relies on end anchorages and grout.
The jacking force is not the design force; losses must be estimated and subtracted to get effective prestress.
Stresses at a section are the sum of axial, prestress bending and load bending terms, f = P/A ± P e y/I ± M y/I.
Load balancing converts a tendon profile into an upward load and makes deflection control intuitive.
Flexural design has two checks: no cracking or limited tension at service, and adequate moment at ultimate.
The end block always needs transverse reinforcement because the anchorage force bursts outward as it spreads.
In continuous beams, cable profile choice controls whether prestress creates reactions, and hence secondary moments.
Partial prestressing is often the economical answer where full prestress would be wasteful or crack control is not critical.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are usually built around computing losses, checking service and ultimate flexure of a given section, and explaining end-block and cable-profile behaviour with a sketch.

bank.q: Explain the principle of prestressing using a simply supported beam carrying a tendon below the axis. Draw the stress diagrams at transfer and at service load, and show why the concrete does not crack in tension.
outline: Tendon force P at eccentricity e gives axial compression P/A and hogging moment P e
Stress at bottom = P/A − P e y/I + M y/I
Choose e so bottom stress stays compressive or zero at service
Contrast with reinforced concrete where tension is carried by cracked steel
Sketch of hogging camber at transfer and downward deflection at load

bank.q: Compare pre-tensioning and post-tensioning with respect to the place of stressing, bond or anchorage action, duct provision, grouting, section sizes and typical products.
outline: Pre-tensioning: long beds, abutments, stressed before casting, bond transfer over transmission length
Post-tensioning: cast with ducts, stressed after hardening, end anchorages and wedges
Grouting only in post-tensioning
Post-tensioning suits long spans and site casting; pre-tensioning suits factory-made units
Table with at least six comparison rows

bank.q: Why must both concrete and steel be of high strength in prestressed construction? Support the answer with the order of magnitude of the stresses involved.
outline: Tendon stress of the order of 1000-1400 N/mm² under working conditions
Concrete must resist high compression and high bearing at anchorages, typically M40 and above
Small sections needed to keep dead load low, so high strength is economical
High bond and anchorage demands, low creep and shrinkage in strong concrete
Danger of splitting if weak concrete is used at anchorages

bank.q: List the losses of prestress in a post-tensioned member and state clearly the stage at which each one occurs.
outline: At transfer: elastic shortening, friction, anchorage slip
With time: creep of concrete, shrinkage of concrete, relaxation of steel
Pre-tensioned members additionally lose from elastic shortening of concrete at transfer
Definition of immediate and deferred losses
Effective force = jacking force minus all losses

bank.q: State the classes of prestressed concrete members used in design and the stress limits that separate them. Explain what decompression means for each class.
outline: Class 1: no tension, section uncracked
Class 2: tension permitted but below the cracking limit, with crack width control
Class 3: cracks permitted within a specified width
Decompression load is where extreme fibre stress is zero
Relation between class, environment exposure and crack control

bank.q: A simply supported post-tensioned beam of span 12 m carries a parabolic tendon with sag 300 mm at midspan and effective prestress 1500 kN. Compute the equivalent upward load from the tendon and the balanced load per metre. State the residual load the beam must carry.
outline: Use w = 8 P e / L²
Substitute P = 1500 kN, e = 0.30 m, L = 12 m
Subtract from applied load to get net downward load
Comment on deflection and on the meaning of full balancing

bank.q: A post-tensioned beam is jacked to 1200 kN. Friction and wobble cause a loss of 6 percent, anchorage slip causes 4 percent, elastic shortening 3 percent, and time-dependent losses total 10 percent of the jacking force. Find the effective prestress and express the answer as a percentage of the jacking force.
outline: Separate immediate and deferred losses
Total loss percentage and arithmetic shown step by step
Effective force = 1200 × (1 − 0.23) = 924 kN
Remark that losses depend on the stage at which percentages are taken
State where each loss acts: along the duct, at anchorage, over full length

bank.q: A rectangular prestressed section 300 mm wide by 700 mm deep carries an effective prestress of 1000 kN at an eccentricity of 200 mm below the axis. The beam supports a service moment of 180 kNm. Compute the extreme fibre stresses and state whether the section is uncracked.
outline: A = 2.1 × 10⁵ mm², I = b D³/12, y = 350 mm
Axial stress P/A
Prestress bending stress P e y / I
Load bending stress M y / I
Combine at top and bottom, check sign convention, conclude on cracking

bank.q: An anchorage applies 800 kN through a bearing plate 250 mm × 250 mm on the end of a 300 mm wide beam. Estimate the bearing stress, and sketch the bursting and spalling zones with the reinforcement you would provide.
outline: Bearing stress = force over plate area, in N/mm²
Compare with the permissible bearing stress in the code
Bursting tension behind the plate, spalling near the loaded face
Closed stirrups and a reinforcement grid in the end block
Primary zone within one beam depth, secondary zone beyond it

bank.q: Explain, with a two-span continuous beam, why a concordant cable gives no reactions from prestress. Use linear transformation to move the cable at the middle support without altering the equivalent loads.
outline: Definition of concordant profile and pressure line
Free reactions are zero when the profile is concordant
Linear transformation shifts the profile by a straight line
Sag between supports is unchanged, so w = 8 P e / L² is unchanged
Shift changes the secondary moments and reactions, so it is used to place concrete cover or control stresses

bank.q: A post-tensioned beam shows fine flexural cracks at service load even though the calculated extreme fibre stress is compressive. Analyse the possible causes and state what you would check.
outline: Losses underestimated, so real effective prestress is lower
Friction and anchorage slip measured values differ along the duct
Creep and shrinkage larger than assumed, relaxation of steel
Temperature and shrinkage restraint stresses not considered
Check grouting, tendon alignment, actual jacking records and crack widths against limits

bank.q: Discuss when partial prestressing should be chosen in place of full prestressing. Compare the two on service stress, crack control, ultimate strength, deflection, and economy for a building floor beam.
outline: Definition of full, limited and partial prestressing
Partial design uses tendons plus conventional rebar
Service: controlled cracking allowed, deflection reduced by both systems
Ultimate: rebar adds ductility, tendon strength still governs
Economy: fewer tendons, smaller anchorages, simpler end blocks
Choice driven by exposure, crack width limits and span

bank.q: Explain why transverse reinforcement is unavoidable in an end block. Derive the nature of bursting stress from the spread of a concentrated force and justify the layout you would adopt.
outline: Concentrated force spreads over about one beam depth
Compatibility of deformation produces transverse tension behind the plate
Spalling stress close to the loaded face
Closed stirrups and grids, placed perpendicular to the force
Bearing plate size reduces both stresses, so check the bearing stress first

bank.q: Compare reinforced concrete and prestressed concrete for a 20 m span pedestrian bridge, covering section depth, dead load, deflection, crack behaviour, construction time and cost in Indian conditions.
outline: Prestressed section is shallower and lighter for the same span
Full compression under service means no cracking and better durability
Camber and deflection control by load balancing
Reinforced option needs much greater depth and deflects more
Cost of jacks, ducts, anchorages and skilled labour against material savings
Conclusion with a reasoned recommendation

glossary.def: Concrete in which an internal compressive stress has been introduced, usually by stretched steel, to oppose the tensile stress from loads.
A group of high-tensile wires, strands or bars used to apply the prestressing force.
Several wires twisted together, commonly seven wires, used as a prestressing tendon.
The force read at the jack when the tendon is tensioned, before any losses.
The force that remains in the tendon after all immediate and time-dependent losses.
The operation of releasing the prestress from the jack or bed into the concrete.
The load at which the stress at the extreme tensile fibre just becomes zero.
The bending moment at which the extreme fibre tensile stress reaches the tensile strength of concrete.
The perpendicular distance between the tendon centroid and the concrete centroidal axis.
The line of action of the resultant compressive force at each section of a prestressed member.
A design method in which the upward force from a curved tendon is balanced against part of the applied load.
A tendon whose profile lies along the pressure line, producing no reactions at the supports.
A straight-line shift of a tendon profile that leaves the equivalent loads and pressure line unchanged.
The moment produced in a continuous member by the reactions that a non-concordant tendon creates at the supports.
A thin metal or plastic sheath cast in concrete to leave a hole for a post-tensioning tendon.
Filling the duct with cement grout after stressing to give bond and protect the tendon from corrosion.
The end device, such as a wedge and plate, that holds the stressed tendon against the concrete.
The region near an anchorage, about one beam depth long, designed for the spreading force.
Transverse tensile stress set up behind an anchorage as the concentrated force spreads into the section.
Transverse tensile stress close to the loaded face, acting near the anchorage plate edges.
Gradual loss of stress in a tendon held at constant length.
Time-dependent shortening of concrete under sustained compressive stress.
Shortening of concrete due to drying, independent of applied stress.
A design in which tendons and ordinary reinforcement together provide the required strength and crack control.
